item.title: China harnesses smart technologies to power transport upgrade
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 08:00:00
A drone photo taken on June 19, 2025 shows smart transport robots at a container terminal of Tianjin Port in north China's Tianjin. (Xinhua/Zhao Zishuo) To drivers crossing the Guandu Yellow River Bridge in central China's Henan Province, it is just routine on a busy highway, but a sophisticated and invisible network of smart digital technologies is hard at work above and below the asphalt. This system was built to meet a very practical challenge. Opened in October 2019, the eight-lane bridge had long faced heavy pressure in terms of maintenance and safety management. To address blind spots, slow response and low efficiency in traditional upkeep, a full-process smart operations model was introduced to manage the bridge. In March 2025, the bridge operator set up a dedicated drone inspection unit equipped with two types of drones. Multi-rotor drones handle detailed checks of bridge surfaces, hazard verification and 3D modeling, while fixed-wing drones cover a 35-kilometer radius in a single flight for long-distance highway patrols. Working alongside road administration teams and manual maintenance crews, the drones form an "air patrol plus ground watch" system intended to provide all-weather, area-wide coverage. The bridge's intelligence capabilities extend beyond aerial patrols. A full-factor digital twin replicates the deck, guardrails, piers and ancillary facilities in a virtual environment. Radar-vision devices help the system detect illegal parking, intrusions and facility abnormalities even at night or in fog. When a risk is identified, alerts are linked to the 3D model and pinpointed to specific locations, replacing the older practice of estimating positions by mile markers. The upgrade is part of a wider push in central China's Henan, which has developed rapid road-condition detection equipment and a smart maintenance platform. Shan Fei, general manager of Henan Transportation Development Research Institute Co., Ltd., said the province has completed digital data collection and 3D modeling for 31,000 kilometers of trunk highways, using positioning from China's BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS) and laser point cloud mapping. The resulting database covers 127 types of assets, including roadbeds, pavements, bridges, tunnels and traffic safety facilities, which he described as China's largest provincial-level digital foundation for highway assets. "From a single milestone or bollard to a kilometer-long bridge or tunnel, every element is now under digital management," Shan said. The Guandu bridge is a microcosm of China's broader push to fuse AI with transportation. According to Liu Wei, China's minister of transport, more than 7,800 kilometers of expressways have undergone digital and intelligent upgrades, 60 automated terminals have been built, and about 27 million pieces of equipment across the sector are now using the BDS. According to the Ministry of Transport, in 2025, 696 long-span bridges crossing rivers, seas and gorges were included in a three-level monitoring network linking national, provincial and individual bridge systems, with basic bridge data and monitoring and alert information shared instantly. Policy support is also expanding. In September 2025, seven government departments, including the Ministry of Transport, issued guidelines on applying AI to transportation, setting out a timetable and roadmap for the sector. In 2026, authorities launched an action plan to create typical application scenarios in areas such as intelligent driving, smart highways, intelligent supervision and smart shipping, aiming to roll out over 100 pilot projects and bring together more than 1,000 innovators. "AI plus transportation has become the new central thread in boosting China's strength in transport," said Wang Yunpeng, chairman of the China Intelligent Transportation Systems Association, noting that a modern, comprehensive, multi-modal transport network is taking shape and accelerating toward digitalization, intelligence, integration and green development.

item.title: China, Europe drive deeper automotive cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 07:53:00
This photo taken on June 2, 2026, shows the view of the Port of Barcelona where cargo ships arrive with fleets of electric cars from China, in Barcelona, Spain. (Photo by Joan Gosa/Xinhua) In October, Stellantis began producing the Leapmotor B10 at its Zaragoza facility in Spain through its partnership with Chinese electric vehicle (EV) maker Leapmotor. The factory had been running at roughly half capacity, a far cry from its peak output of about 470,000 vehicles in 2019. Stellantis needed to fill its production lines; Leapmotor needed a European base. Neither side called it a favor. The arrangement exemplifies deepening cooperation between China and Europe in the automotive industry, fueled by consumer demand and manufacturers' commercial calculations alike. Analysts say this industrial partnership is more than a stopgap measure, with considerable potential to deliver mutual benefits. People visit the exhibition zone of Leapmotor at the 2025 IAA Mobility in Munich, Germany, Sept. 10, 2025. (Xinhua/Zhang Fan) CONSUMER VERDICT Chinese cars are gaining popularity across Europe, offering competitive specifications at attractive prices. Chinese brands have targeted a segment that legacy automakers have been slow to serve: drivers who previously owned BMWs, Mercedes-Benzes or Range Rovers. According to one dealership in West London, about three in five buyers of Chinese cars previously owned a luxury brand. Luis Murias, general manager of Spanish automotive data platform DAT, attributes the success of Chinese cars to multiple factors, including "industrial restructuring, commitment, overall quality improvement, competitive features and warranty, and progress in safety standards." A May survey of young Italian consumers by consulting and market research firm Arete Methodos found that 53 percent of respondents are most attracted by the combination of technological features and product quality of Chinese cars -- outnumbering the 43 percent who cite their competitive prices as decisive. In recent years, Chinese car makers have accelerated localization. Ten European production plans have been announced since September 2023, advisory company AutoMotion reported, including BYD's first European plant in Szeged, Hungary and SAIC's 200 million-euro (222.7 million U.S. dollars) factory in Spain's Galicia. This photo taken on Jan. 2, 2025 shows a showroom of Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng in Oslo, capital of Norway. (Xinhua/Zhang Yuliang) SUPPLY-SIDE LOGIC Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) -- a cheaper, longer-lasting battery chemistry that underpins most affordable EVs -- is forecast to rise from around 10 percent of the European battery market today to between 40 and 60 percent by 2030, yet Europe has no operational plants to make it. In September, Gotion High-tech, a Chinese battery manufacturer, agreed to invest around 1.1 billion euros (about 1.23 billion dollars) for a 49 percent stake in Volkswagen's battery-cell plant in Sagunto, Spain. The partnership reflects a complementary division of role. Gotion contributes LFP technology, manufacturing processes and raw material supply chains. PowerCo, Volkswagen's battery subsidiary, brings its European industrial footprint, logistics and regulatory expertise. Javier Rivera, chief financial officer of PowerCo Battery Spain, described the relationship as having evolved "from supplier to technology partner and now to industrial partner." Michael Schumann, chairman of the Board of the German Federal Association for Economic Development and Foreign Trade, told Xinhua that German companies remain active in China. A May 2026 flash survey by the German Chamber of Commerce in China found that the share of companies planning to increase their investments in China over the next two years reached its highest level since 2023. He also pointed to a remarkable shift: German headquarters are increasingly learning from their Chinese operations, not the other way around. "Today, the transformation of the automotive industry, particularly the shift towards electric mobility and software-defined vehicles, is creating new forms of competition and cooperation between German and Chinese companies," Schumann added. "No single country has ever been able to dominate or capture the entire market. As a leading technology company, BYD will bring relevant technologies to Europe," said BYD Executive Vice President Li Ke. "We will grow here and help the local supply chain transition to next-generation suppliers, making important contributions to the local economy." People visit the pavilion of Chinese carmaker Leapmotor at the 2024 Paris Motor Show during the media day in Paris, France, Oct. 14, 2024. (Xinhua/Gao Jing) REBALANCING THROUGH COMPLEMENTARITY The automotive sector attracted more Chinese Foreign Direct Investment in 2025 than any other industry in Europe. Investments in the sector totaled 7.6 billion euros (8.5 billion dollars), with 93 percent of them focused on the EV supply chain, according to a report by Rhodium Group and MERICS. "Europe has a great tradition in design," Andrea Levy, president of the Turin Auto Show, told Xinhua, adding that cooperation can combine different strengths and contribute to better vehicles. Industry insiders believe that the pairing is no temporary arrangement. "China Speed is not a cultural phenomenon, but the result of clear decisions regarding product design, portfolio complexity, and the supplier base," said Oliver Knapp, a partner at global management consultancy Roland Berger. "And that is precisely why parts of it can also be implemented in Europe." Alexandre Marian, a partner at AlixPartners, depicted the Stellantis-Leapmotor deal as a "reverse joint venture," in which European manufacturers seek alliances to learn Chinese EV know-how. "If our (Stellantis and Leapmotor) partnership is the strategy, Zaragoza is the proof that we can combine global technology, competitiveness and European industrial capabilities," said Stellantis representative Silvia Vernetti.

item.title: Why has the CPC succeeded? The fifth plenary session provides a window of observation: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 00:51:00
The view of Beijing's Central Business District Photo: VCG How has this massive party of unprecedented scale demonstrated formidable organizational mobilization and implementation capacity when confronted with major risks and challenges? When the international community turns its attention to the fifth plenary session, it is not just observing China's politics; more importantly, it seeks insights from "China's governance" for political party building, national governance across the world, and even the reform of the global governance system. The 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC) is holding its fifth plenary session in Beijing from October 26 to 29 to deliberate on major issues concerning the continued advancement of full and rigorous Party self-governance. Marking the 105th anniversary of the founding of the CPC and the launch year of the 15th Five-Year Plan, this plenary session draws global attention to the underlying foundations of China's development. Particularly against the backdrop of partisan politics in many countries being mired in polarized, fragmented and chaotic contests, with many ruling parties feeling helpless in the face of social division and stalled development at home, why does China present a completely different picture? The fifth plenary session serves as an important window for the world to gain insights. For anyone following China, today's China is defined not merely by economic growth, technological breakthroughs and landmark projects. The robust organizational capacity and political strength underpinning these remarkable achievements further illuminate the source of China's steady progress amid profound changes of the times. As the largest governing party in the world, the CPC maintains solidarity and unity at all times. How has this massive party of unprecedented scale demonstrated formidable organizational mobilization and implementation capacity when confronted with major risks and challenges? When the international community turns its attention to the fifth plenary session, it is not just observing China's politics; more importantly, it seeks insights from "China's governance" for political party building, national governance across the world, and even the reform of the global governance system. An increasing number of insightful observers around the world have identified a clear thread running through China's development: The leadership of the CPC has consistently served as the central pillar underpinning the steady advancement of the country's various undertakings and is the master key to unlocking the secret behind the success of "the governance of China." Persistently advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance constitutes the fundamental mechanism at the heart of this master key. Since the 18th CPC National Congress, the great new project of Party building in the new era has been advanced in depth. China has continuously intensified its fight against corruption, improved its intra-Party oversight system, and made sustained efforts to enhance Party conduct through regular and long-term mechanisms. These efforts have included combating formalism and bureaucratism, holding officials accountable for dereliction of duty and failure to fulfill their responsibilities, and encouraging officials to take initiative and fulfill their duties. Such measures have helped ensure that decisions and plans made by the central leadership are effectively implemented at all levels and that resources and efforts from across society remain consistently directed toward shared goals. This political courage to turn the blade inward and confront problems within the Party itself is rarely seen in the history of political parties worldwide. For a long time, many voices in international public discourse have taken it for granted that there are only a handful of established models for building a governing party, as though effective governance could be achieved only by replicating certain institutional frameworks. China has challenged these conventional assumptions with verifiable development data. One of the most tangible outcomes of these measures is that public trust in the ruling party in China has remained consistently high for many years. Meanwhile, the efficiency with which major national strategies are implemented and the continuity of public policy execution have gained widespread international recognition. The principle that the governance over the Party must precede the governance of the country is grounded in concrete and profound practical realities. In today's international community, a stark contrast has emerged between "China's governance" and "the West's chaos." Some Western countries that firmly believe in multiparty systems and the separation of powers are mired in intensified partisan conflicts and frequent changes of government. Internal political polarization is escalating, societal divisions are deepening, and public policies fluctuate under the tug-of-war of interest groups, making it difficult to reach consensus even on basic livelihood issues. Some Western scholars, after comparing the party politics of major powers, have had to admit that "the CPC possesses strong governing capacity." In recent years, party representatives from various regions, including Southeast Asia, Africa, Europe, and Latin America, have come to China to study and learn from the governance experiences of the CPC through inter-party exchanges. China's long-term approach to development, strategic vision, and practical achievements have opened up broader intellectual space for countries to independently explore political development paths that align with their own national conditions. The world today needs truly effective governance solutions more than ever. An increasing number of countries and political parties are drawing inspiration from "China's governance" to explore governance paths that suit their own national situations. This not only provides more diverse practical solutions for the global governance system but also strengthens the consensus among countries to collectively address global challenges. It is also the precious public value contributed by China through its unwavering efforts to promote full and rigorous Party self-governance amid a world marked by intertwined changes and turmoil.

item.title: Key plenum to advance full, rigorous Party self-governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 00:04:00
Photo:Xinhua The 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC) started its fifth plenary session in Beijing on Monday morning. Xi Jinping, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, delivered a work report on behalf of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and expounded on a draft decision of the CPC Central Committee on some major issues concerning strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance, according to the Xinhua News Agency. The draft decision summarizes the achievements and experience of full and rigorous Party self-governance in the new era in a truth-seeking manner, and offers in-depth analysis of the situation and tasks concerning Party building at present and for some time to come. It also sets out strategic plans for strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance, according to a Political Bureau meeting in September that decided to submit the document to the plenum for review, Xinhua reported. Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the full and rigorous Party self-governance has made significant progress, opened up a new frontier for the century-old Party in self-reform, and brought about historic achievements and transformations in the cause of the Party and the country, said an earlier Political Bureau meeting in July that set the plenum's agenda. The meeting said the Party and the people have won the historical initiative to build a strong Party and country, but noted that as profound changes unfold in the world, in China and within the Party, efforts to exercise full and rigorous Party self-governance also face many new circumstances and challenges. It called for adopting higher standards and taking more concrete measures to uphold and apply the valuable experience of full and rigorous Party self-governance in the new era, resolve the prominent issues facing Party building, and consolidate and develop the sound political environment created through Party self-supervision and self-governance. Chinese observers said the plenum underscores the CPC's determination to sustain rigorous Party self-governance as China enters a crucial stage of its modernization drive. Maintaining effective governance requires the Party to continuously address the challenges faced by the CPC, while ensuring that institutional reforms translate into stronger governance capacity, sustained economic and social development, and tangible improvements in people's lives. Maintaining vigor As China enters the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), a critical stage in laying the groundwork for basically achieving socialist modernization by 2035, the CPC faces severe challenges: strengthening its governing capacity, staying connected with the people, guarding against complacency and resolutely combating corruption, read a Xinhua commentary. Only through strong Party leadership and unwavering commitment to full and rigorous self-governance can central leadership decisions be fully implemented and the country's long-term development stay on course. History has shown that maintaining rigorous Party governance requires a long-term commitment, particularly in the fight against corruption. Any relaxation or inconsistency in anti-corruption efforts risks allowing entrenched problems to resurface, potentially undermining years of progress, Dong Yu, executive vice dean of the China Institute for Development Planning at Tsinghua University, told the Global Times. For China to achieve its long-term modernization goals, preventing corruption from taking root is therefore not merely a matter of political discipline, but a broader governance imperative, said Dong, noting that seen in this light, China's continued anti-corruption drive is about more than addressing immediate problems. It is also an effort to strengthen the institutional foundations needed to sustain the country's development over the long term. In December 2012, the CPC central leadership introduced a code of conduct, known as "eight-point rules," in a bid to strengthen Party self-governance. It established regulations for Party leaders regarding research tours, meetings, documentation, and other official duties, cracking down on lavish banquets, red carpet events, pomp, entourages, unnecessary meetings, and luxury perks that had once been regarded by some as typical symbols of power. It has become a cornerstone of the CPC's efforts to ensure integrity, discipline and public trust. Also since 2012, the Party has pressed ahead with a rigorous anti-corruption campaign targeting high-ranking officials, misconduct at the grassroots level and corruption involving officials who have fled overseas. Some of the most senior officials - including former members of the Political Bureau and its Standing Committee, top military brass, and retirees who left their leading positions years ago -- have been brought to justice, according to an article by Xinhua. In its crackdown on high-ranking officials, commonly known as "hunting tigers", more than 500 centrally managed officials were placed under investigation between the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012 and the eve of the 20th CPC National Congress in 2022. The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision (NCS) launched investigations into 87 such officials in 2023, 92 in 2024 and 181 in 2025, according to an article published by Xinhua on Monday. The campaign has also targeted lower-level corruption, an effort known as "swatting flies". In 2025 alone, the CCDI and NCS directly investigated or oversaw 8,116 cases involving misconduct and corruption affecting ordinary people. Nationwide, authorities investigated 967,000 such cases, imposed disciplinary penalties on 627,000 people and referred 22,000 people to prosecutors, according to the Xinhua report. Rigorous Party self-governance is intended to strengthen the CPC's governing capacity by addressing practical challenges, refining its approach to governance and improving its ability to navigate risks, advance reforms and pursue the country's modernization goals, Zhuang Deshui, deputy director of the Research Center for Government Integrity-Building at Peking University, told the Global Times. Zhuang said the broader aim is to ensure that the Party retains the resilience, political judgment and strategic foresight needed to make consequential decisions shaping China's future and the lives of its people at critical moments in history. To strengthen full and rigorous Party self-governance, upholding the Party's overall leadership is imperative, analysts said. Over the past years, the strong leadership of the CPC has been the key to China's great achievements in such fields as economic, scientific and social development. Latest official data released showed China's GDP grew 4.6 percent year-on- year in the first three quarters of this year, as the economy maintained steady growth under pressure and continued shifting toward new growth drivers. Meanwhile, the country has also achieved significant results in green transformation in recent years, including building the world's largest and most complete clean energy industrial chain, with green and low-carbon industries becoming an important engine of economic growth. Last month, the 134.2-kilometer Pinglu Canal, stretching from Hengzhou in South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region to the Beibu Gulf, officially opened. It is the first nationally planned and coordinated canal project since 1949 to connect an inland river with the sea, providing southwestern China with its shortest, most cost-effective and most convenient route to the sea. Global significance By steadily tackling these problems faced by the CPC, China is also creating a more transparent environment for international cooperation. The "rigorousness" in official documents must be translated into a level playing field where merit and the rule of law prevail over connections and bribery. It is hardly surprising that many foreign observers have said that the CPC's ability to reform itself is a key factor in its success, reads the Xinhua commentary. The 20th Central Committee of the CPC's fifth plenary session has also been closely watched by foreign media outlets, with some focused more on the Party discipline theme of this session. International attention to the fifth plenary session reflects more than an interest in the country's domestic politics. It also points to growing concerns over the limitations of established governance models worldwide. Against this backdrop, China's emphasis on long-term strategic planning and policy continuity has drawn attention, particularly among other countries grappling with their own governance challenges and exploring alternative approaches, said Chinese experts. Many governance challenges around the world arise not because countries lack policies, but because institutions lack effectiveness, coordination, or public confidence. The Chinese experience suggests that governance capacity depends not only on economic resources but also on institutional discipline, accountability, and the ability to adapt to changing circumstances, Essam Sharaf, former Egyptian Prime Minister, told the Global Times in a previous interview. One of the most important lessons is that self-renewal is essential for long-term success. Institutions must regularly evaluate their performance, address shortcomings, and pursue continuous improvement. Without such efforts, even capable systems may struggle to sustain effectiveness over time, said Sharaf. "From my observations, one 'secret' of the CPC is the professionalism of officials, which is not limited to senior leaders. High-quality public management is pervasive. The CPC Central Committee's Organization Department is responsible for selecting, training, monitoring, assessing, and promoting Party and government officials - and, when necessary, demoting or firing them. The process is rigorous, quantitative and continuous," Robert Lawrence Kuhn, chairman of The Kuhn Foundation, creator and host of Closer to Truth, and a recipient of the China Reform Friendship Medal, told the Xinhua News Agency in an interview. "CPC rules on work style and personal conduct have become stricter. The Eight Rules of the Party Central Committee reject extravagance and reduce ceremonial visits, meetings and 'empty talk'. A training campaign emphasizes strict standards in morality, power and self-discipline, as well as integrity in decision-making, official conduct and personal behavior. Over more than 35 years of engaging with Chinese officials at all levels, I have generally found them to be among the most competent administrators anywhere," said Kuhn. The CPC's experience offers a valuable lesson for political parties around the world, particularly those that have governed for extended periods: sustaining effective governance depends not merely on organizational strength or institutional arrangements, but also on the ability to identify shortcomings, correct mistakes and continuously renew themselves, said Dong. The effectiveness of the CPC's self-reform and strict Party governance should therefore be assessed not only through institutional changes, but also through their tangible outcomes. The key is whether these efforts have strengthened governance, advanced economic and social development, and improved people's lives, Dong noted.

item.title: Why is Philippine coast guard spokesman wading into education?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 22:50:00
Philippine Coast Guard spokesman Jay Tarriela. Photo:VCG Soon after US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth branded Confucius Institutes a "threat to national security," Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) spokesman Jay Tarriela wasted no time echoing this claim. An official meant to focus on maritime law enforcement is now pushing the confrontational rhetoric into education and culture. On Sunday local time, Tarriela reposted Hegseth's remarks about Confucius Institutes, claiming that these institutes have a mission of "infiltrating the minds of students." He suggested that the same phenomenon is happening in the Philippines and declared that "Beijing's campaign against the Philippines is not waged only at sea. It is also waged in classrooms." What makes these remarks striking is not only the accusations against Chinese educational and cultural exchanges but also the figure making them. At first glance, one might mistake Tarriela for "the Philippine defense secretary" or "foreign secretary." In reality, he is merely the spokesman for the PCG. Something rather peculiar seems to be happening in Philippine politics. Officials responsible for maritime law enforcement are not content to limit themselves to maritime affairs. They are also weighing in on education, culture and diplomacy, even presuming to decide what kinds of knowledge pose a "national security threat." Tarriela's personal political ambitions appear to be outgrowing the boundaries of his official role. Tarriela appears increasingly comfortable with the attention this expanded role brings him. He has repeatedly singled out China for criticism on social media and now parrots Washington's rhetoric over Confucius Institutes, injecting it into the Philippine education debate. His public interventions are swelling well beyond maritime affairs. His career path raises a broader question about the incentives that shape promotions within the Philippine bureaucracy. Routine maritime patrols, rescue operations, and professional capacity-building seem to attract far less attention than drama. Officials who prioritize political theater and confrontational rhetoric more readily rise to prominence, gaining public visibility, influence and, potentially, career advancement. However, the Philippines as a whole is paying a price. Its room for diplomatic maneuver is shrinking, anti-China sentiment is intensifying, maritime tensions are becoming harder to defuse, and disputes that could otherwise be settled through negotiation are increasingly framed as all-or-nothing battles over sovereignty. Are the Philippines' foreign and defense policies - and figures like Tarriela - truly protecting the country's national interests, or are they exposing it to greater geopolitical risks? Over the past few months, the US-based think tank SeaLight and Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr have taken turns criticizing Chinese-language education and cultural exchange programs in the Philippines. They suggested that educational exchanges could be used for intelligence gathering, even as Teodoro stopped short of saying that any wrongdoing had been proven. The fallout was immediate: Roughly 150 to 180 Chinese teachers in the Philippines reportedly left due to safety concerns. What should have been bridges of educational and cultural exchange were instead dragged onto the front lines of geopolitical rivalry. What, exactly, makes an institution that teaches Chinese languages, organizes paper-cutting activities and promotes cultural exchange a "national security threat" capable of "infiltrating" American and Filipino minds? This argument turns cultural exchange into a tool of cognitive warfare, implying that learning Chinese or seeking to understand China amounts to being "brainwashed." If applied consistently, the same logic would brand virtually any foreign language or cultural program a security threat. The US itself runs an extensive network of cultural and educational exchange programs around the world. By the same reasoning, does learning English amount to American brainwashing? The Philippines' diplomatic relations with China remain sound, said Malacanang Palace lately. That statement suggests that Manila is well aware that improving relations with Beijing serves the interests of both countries. Existing differences should not be exploited to manufacture lasting hostility, stifle diplomacy, or justify unconditional dependence on Washington. When a PCG spokesman can so readily import the US Department of War's absurd security claims into Philippine classrooms, and when taking a hard line against China becomes a potential career fast track, the real damage is not that Filipinos are supposedly having their minds "infiltrated." It is that the Philippines risks trading its limited diplomatic rationality, flexibility and economic opportunities for ever-louder slogans, increasingly fragile relations with its neighbors, and an ever-narrower range of choices.

item.title: India's baseless patrol accusations against Chinese military 'a tactical maneuver for domestic politics': expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 22:12:00
china india China strictly abides by the relevant agreements and common understandings reached between the two countries, and conducts normal border patrol and control activities to safeguard its territorial sovereignty and stability in the border areas, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular press conference on Monday. Guo made the remarks in response to India's accusations that Chinese military has disturbed the peace along the border. A spokesman from India's Ministry of External Affairs claimed that such disturbances occur when Chinese forces "diverge from established patterns." Guo stressed that China and India maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels. We hope that India will work with China in the same direction by jointly implementing the common understandings reached between the two sides and maintaining peace and tranquility in the border areas with concrete actions, the spokesperson added. The Chinese Foreign Ministry's response followed claims by Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, who said on Friday that the situation along the China-India border was disturbed from time to time "when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns," according to a report by Indian media outlet NDTV. Jaiswal also indicated that both sides continued to use existing diplomatic and military mechanisms to resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC). Jaiswal's claims were preceded by remarks from Indian border police official Shatrujeet Kapur, who said on Thursday that face-offs between Indian and Chinese personnel had occurred at several locations along the border areas and were continuing, according to Indian media reports. The Indian side's unsubstantiated public accusations represented a calculated tactical maneuver over patrol issues, partly reflecting domestic political considerations while leaving room for further discussions through existing diplomatic and military channels, Qian Feng, director of the Research Department at Tsinghua University's National Strategy Institute, told the Global Times. To prevent border issues from disrupting the improving momentum in bilateral relations, India should abide by existing border management agreements and implement the consensus reached by the two leaders during their meeting in New Delhi, Qian noted. Both sides should continue to rely on established diplomatic and military communication mechanisms to manage differences, avoid misunderstandings that could affect broader bilateral ties. On September 12, the leaders of China and India met on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, where they reached the important consensus that China and India should be partners, according to the Xinhua News Agency. The Chinese side urged both sides to pursue parallel progress in bilateral ties and border issues, with the two tracks reinforcing each other, so as to maintain peace and tranquility in border areas. To prevent individual border disputes from affecting broader bilateral relations, Border issues should be addressed through established mechanisms, including talks between the special representatives from the two countries, rather than allowing isolated disputes to affect the overall relationship, Qian said. He noted that meanwhile, both sides should expand practical cooperation in less sensitive areas to offset the negative impact of differences and encourage a more rational public understanding of bilateral relations. Stable China-India relations would help unlock the cooperation potential of the two major economies, reduce strategic pressures on both sides and contribute to peace and development in Asia, while strengthening cooperation among Global South countries, Qian said.

item.title: GT Voice: Rare-earth metal recycling should not be driven by geopolitics
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 22:05:00
Rare earth File photo:VCG An American recycling company is recovering rare-earth metals from old wind turbines, which The Wall Street Journal said over the weekend could be one part of a drive to help reduce US reliance on China for the materials. While recycling critical materials from retired equipment can tap existing resources, treating rare-earth magnet recycling as a breakthrough to achieve critical minerals "self-sufficiency" or framing it as a shortcut to shake off reliance on China's supply chain, seriously underestimates industrial realities. Rare-earth metals are widely used in wind power systems, new-energy vehicles and high-end manufacturing, serving as core components of the modern industrial system. As these industries expand, recycling materials from old equipment has broad long-term potential. But being technically recoverable is not the same as being commercially viable and capable of stable industrial supply. The disassembly, separation and purification of wind turbines involve highly complex processes, which place high demands on specialized equipment, technical expertise and environmental protection treatment. Once transportation, labor and processing costs are added up, whether recycled products can compete with existing supplies on price and quality still has to be tested by the market. An even trickier hurdle lies in the stability of the feedstock. Wind turbines are generally engineered for service lives of more than two decades. Most large-scale wind farms installed across Europe and the US came online only in the past decade, so very few turbines have reached retirement age. Even if some turbines are replaced with better models, recyclers may still face uneven, scattered and non-standardized feedstock. Without reliable raw material inflows, downstream separation and refining lines cannot run at full capacity, economies of scale remain out of reach, and unit costs stay high. This means recycling can serve as a valuable supplement to critical mineral supplies, but it cannot replace mature supply chains any time soon. In recent years, some Western countries have repeatedly discussed critical mineral security and rolled out multiple policy initiatives, but actual progress has been relatively limited. The problem is not a lack of political will but the fact that building industrial chains follows its own logic. The global supply of critical minerals is never an isolated contest over a single link or a single technology. It is a systemic ecosystem integrating resources, technical expertise, cost control, skilled talent, specialized equipment and downstream market support. Mine development involves long investment cycles, separation and purification pose high technical barriers, and downstream manufacturing requires decades of accumulated experience. A shortfall in any single link will drag down the entire industrial chain. Recycling and refining are never simple matters of technological breakthroughs. The chain equally requires a complete process system, stable raw material supply and a sustainable business model, all of which are necessary. Treating recycling as a shortcut to bypass existing mature supply chains underestimates the systemic difficulty of industrial chain construction. China's rare-earth industry took shape over decades of steady accumulation. Yet today, some economies enjoy the benefits of the global division of labor while framing normal supply relationships as risks and seeking to sever industrial chains. Meanwhile, there is no such thing as a shortcut in the global critical mineral industrial chain. The formation of a mature industrial system is the long-term combined result of resource endowment, technology accumulation, market scale and cost structure. It cannot be completely rearranged by a few technological breakthroughs or several policy measures. China's rare-earth export measures are fully reasonable and compliant and have long provided stable, reliable supplies for related industries across the world. By hyping "reducing dependence on China," some economies appear to be pursuing supply chain security; in reality they are narrowing their own path of development. Supply chain security can never be achieved through artificial fragmentation. Overall, recycling rare-earth metals from old wind turbines is a worthwhile pursuit within the circular economy, but it should be judged as a supplementary industrial strategy - not burdened with geopolitical expectations.

item.title: 2,054 aftershocks recorded after magnitude-7.0 earthquake in Baqen as geo-analysis on 80 glacial lakes and 145 glaciers unfolds
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 20:13:00
Power workers install electricity connections for prefabricated shelters at a temporary relocation site in Maru Township, Baqen County in Southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, on October 25, 2026. Photo: IC Following the magnitude-7.0 earthquake in Baqen County of the city of Nagqu, Southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, 2,054 aftershocks had been recorded as of Monday morning. Rescue and relief operations are progressing steadily to ensure basic food and water supplies and support the orderly resumption of normal life and production in affected areas, China Central Television (CCTV) reported on Monday. According to the China Earthquake Networks Center, among the aftershocks, 10 measured magnitude-4.0 to -4.9, and two measured magnitude-5.0 to -5.9. No aftershocks of magnitude-6.0 or above had been recorded. The strongest aftershock measured magnitude-5.7, with its epicenter 19 kilometers from that of the main quake. Rescue operations are progressing steadily. The Chinese People's Armed Police Force Xizang Corps has searched 475 households across seven villages in the Maru Township area as of 3 pm Sunday and provided medical assistance. Rescue workers continue to provide hot meals and drinking water to affected residents, meeting their basic needs and supporting the orderly restoration of normal life and production in the earthquake-hit areas. Gangqie Township, one of the areas hit hardest by the earthquake, is stepping up efforts to relocate affected residents and distribute cold-weather supplies. Seventeen temporary shelters have accommodated more than 900 households. At a temporary shelter in a village in Gangqie Township, 200 prefabricated houses are being built to ensure that affected residents can move in as soon as possible. Local authorities have also deployed emergency teams to inspect buildings, identify safety hazards and classify damaged homes, providing a basis for future repairs and reconstruction. Peng Jie, a volunteer from South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region who traveled for two nights and three days to reach the earthquake-hit area in Xizang, told the Global Times on Monday that he arrived on Sunday and spent the night in his own tent, enduring temperatures of around -10C. With the initial search-and-rescue operations largely completed, relief efforts have shifted toward providing shelter and daily necessities for affected residents. Drawing on his experience as a survivor of the magnitude-8.0 quake that hit Wenchuan of Sichuan in 2008, Peng said he hopes to provide psychological support to survivors, many of whom may be struggling with anxiety over aftershocks or the loss of family members. He plans to share practical safety advice on how to respond to aftershocks. Through one-on-one conversations and emotional support, he hopes to help affected residents overcome their fears and regain confidence, Peng said. Following the Baqen earthquake, China's Ministry of Natural Resources has completed inspections of potential geological hazard sites within 50 kilometers of the earthquake's epicenter and is continuing to monitor the risk of secondary geological disasters, CCTV reported on Monday. The ministry has activated a Level III geological disaster response and sent additional experts to the earthquake-hit area to assess potential secondary geological hazards with local teams. Remote-sensing analysis of 80 glacial lakes and 145 glaciers within 50 kilometers of the affected area found that the earthquake had limited overall impacts on them, with no earthquake-triggered glacial lake outburst disasters detected so far.

item.title: A cyclone to hit Himalayas and bring extreme snowfall to Xizang region? China's meteorological authority debunks rumors
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 14:31:00
Sunrise over the snow-capped peaks of the Himalayas Photo: IC The China Meteorological Administration (CMA) on Monday debunked online claims that a tropical cyclone forming over the Bay of Bengal between October 26 and October 31 would "slam into the Himalayas" and bring exceptionally heavy snowfall to the southwestern part of China's Xizang Autonomous Region, clarifying that the storm could affect southern Xizang but that the description of the online claims was inaccurate. According to Dong Lin, chief forecaster at China's National Meteorological Center (NMC), a tropical depression is currently active over the Bay of Bengal and is expected to intensify into a cyclonic storm on Monday, with its strength comparable to the tropical storm category used in China. After forming, the storm is forecast to move westward initially and continue to intensify, potentially reaching the level of a very severe cyclonic storm, with sustained winds of 33 to 38 meters per second. The storm is expected to make landfall along India's eastern coast on October 28 as a severe or very severe cyclonic storm before turning northward and gradually weakening, chinanews.com.cn reported. Given the limitations of the forecast period, forecasts of the storm's post-landfall track and intensity remain uncertain. By the time it approaches the Himalayas, the system is expected to have weakened into a weak residual vortex, making online claims that the cyclone will "slam into" the Himalayas inaccurate, and its main body is impossible to cross the mountain range, Dong said. The NMC forecasts notable rain and snow across central and eastern Xizang on Friday and Saturday as a Bay of Bengal storm moves northward and interacts with a plateau trough. Shannan Prefecture, Xigaze and Lhasa in Xizang could see moderate to heavy snow or sleet, while parts of the southern border may experience heavy to exceptionally heavy snowfall, with 10 to 30 millimeters of precipitation and 5 to 25 centimeters of new snow accumulation. According to Chen Tao, chief forecaster from the NMC, the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau's high terrain acts as a natural barrier, preventing the Bay of Bengal storm from crossing it. The heavy precipitation and snow forecast for southern Xizang is not directly attributable to the cyclone itself crossing the mountains, Chen told the Global Times on Monday. Chen explained that on Friday and Saturday, the circulation of the northward-moving Bay of Bengal storm is expected to drive southerly winds, continuously transporting warm, moist air toward the plateau. When this moisture encounters the southern slopes of the Himalayas, it will be forced upward. The orographic uplift along the southern slopes of the Himalayas will trigger heavy rain and snow. An eastward-moving westerly trough is expected to interact with the Bay of Bengal storm, boosting moisture transport and atmospheric uplift and intensifying precipitation. The storm's circulation is forecast to weaken on November 1, bringing a significant reduction in rain and snow across southern Xizang, Chen said. According to Chen, the storm's evolution will be influenced by the westerly trough, the subtropical high and South Asia's terrain. If it weakens rapidly after landfall, reduced moisture transport could alter the intensity and distribution of precipitation in southern Xizang, requiring continuous monitoring and updated forecasts. According to Dong, whether heavy snowfall occurs in southwestern Xizang will depend not only on the cyclone's track but also on the strength and position of the plateau trough, the residual vortex's intensity and moisture transport efficiency. As the forecast period is relatively long, the actual snowfall intensity and accumulation remain uncertain.

item.title: China's state security authority warns of data security risks from discarded industrial equipment
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 09:45:00
Photo: China's Ministry of State Security China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) warned on its WeChat account on Monday that improperly disposed-of industrial equipment and specialized instruments could pose risks to commercial secrets, critical infrastructure and national security, as sensitive data may remain recoverable even after files are deleted or storage devices are formatted. According to the article the MSS posted, some organizations mistakenly believe that deleting files or formatting hard drives is sufficient before selling or disposing of outdated equipment. However, such operations generally remove only file indexes, leaving underlying data potentially recoverable through specialized techniques. Conventional file deletion or formatting does not necessarily erase the underlying information, the article noted. Even equipment that appears to have reached the end of its service life may still contain sensitive corporate or industry data. The risks vary across sectors, potentially affecting corporate interests, the security of critical industries and national security, according to the article. In critical infrastructure sectors such as energy, telecommunications, transportation, chemicals and water management, retired industrial control systems and programmable controllers may contain operational parameters, facility layouts and security configurations. If acquired by overseas organizations, such information could be used to identify system vulnerabilities and security weaknesses, potentially facilitating cyberattacks or physical sabotage, the MSS warned. The article also highlighted risks associated with secondhand surveying and monitoring equipment, including GPS receivers and geological exploration instruments. Such devices may retain high-precision coordinates, terrain data and mineral exploration records, potentially including sensitive geographical information related to military-controlled areas, classified facilities and strategic infrastructure projects, the MSS said. Foreign intelligence agencies could also seek to acquire discarded industrial equipment and storage media from sensitive sectors through secondhand trading platforms or recycling channels, the article warned. Such equipment could be used to recover sensitive information or reverse-engineer system architectures, control logic and security vulnerabilities. Some buyers may offer unusually high prices while specifically targeting industrial enterprises and research institutions. To mitigate these risks, the article called for stricter management of discarded equipment, emphasizing that secure data destruction should take place before devices are sold or transferred. For equipment containing critical data, physical degaussing or destruction of storage media should be prioritized to prevent information recovery, according to the article. The article also recommended using qualified recycling and disposal providers rather than casually selling industrial equipment through secondhand platforms, while ensuring that the disposal process is properly documented. It further urged organizations to exercise caution when approached by buyers offering unusually high prices for discarded equipment, and to verify their identities and qualifications. Global Times
